findings.situation: On a married filing jointly return, only the spouse is a New York public employee with 414(h) contributions on a W-2, so the filer answers 'no' about themself.
findings.source_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 21: "enter the amount of 414(h) retirement contributions, if shown on any federal Form W-2"
findings.why: The addition covers 414(h) contributions on any W-2 included in the return, including a spouse's on a joint return. The question asks only about 'you', so it can miss a spouse's contributions.

findings.situation: A New York public employee has 414(h) contributions on a W-2 but does not belong to any of the listed retirement systems or programs.
findings.source_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 21: "enter the amount ... if you are: – a member of the New York State and Local Retirement Systems ... – a member of the New York State Teachers' Retirement System; – an employee of the State or City University of New York who belongs to the Optional Retirement Program; – a member of the New York City Employees' Retirement System ... or – a member of the Manhattan and Bronx Surface Transit Operating Authority (MABSTOA) Pension Plan."
findings.why: The question ('Are you a public employee of New York State or its local governments with 414(h) retirement contributions shown on a Form W-2?') does not require membership in one of the listed systems. That condition appears only in the help text, so a filer who is not a member can still truthfully answer yes.

findings.situation: A filer used a NY 529 withdrawal to pay K-12 private school tuition, or moved the account to another state's 529 program, and answers no because federal 529 rules treat these as qualified, but the line needs a yes.
findings.source_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 22: "Nonqualified withdrawals from a New York 529 college savings program include, but are not limited to: • the transfer to another state's program ... • any withdrawal used to pay tuition and related expenses in connection with enrollment or attendance at elementary or secondary public, private, or religious schools"
findings.why: The question and help use the term "nonqualified" but do not give New York's definition. A filer who knows the federal meaning would leave out K-12 tuition, transfers to another state's plan, and pre-September 5, 2024 loan payments or Roth rollovers, which New York counts as nonqualified.

findings.situation: A filer whose withdrawal was made because the beneficiary died or became disabled, or who transferred funds between family members' accounts within New York's program, may answer yes, but these do not trigger the Line 22 worksheet.
findings.source_text: ny_it201i p. 8: "considered nonqualified unless it is used: ... for any purpose, provided the withdrawal is the result of the death or disability of the designated beneficiary"; "Transfers between accounts of family members that are not disbursed in cash or in-kind within New York's program are not considered distributions"
findings.why: The question does not say that these withdrawals and transfers are excluded. A filer could treat a non-education withdrawal or an account transfer as a nonqualified withdrawal and wrongly open the gate.

findings.situation: A filer kept a New York abode for all of 2025 except a stretch shorter than half a month (or for more than half of every month), so truthfully answers yes, yet every month counts as a full month and the chart amount needs no proration.
findings.source_text: ny_it201i p. 18, Line 59: "(Count any period you maintained the abode for more than one-half of a month as one month.)"
findings.why: The question asks only whether the abode covered part of the year. It does not apply the half-month rule, so the gate fires when the prorated months would be 12 and the chart amount stands unchanged.

findings.situation: A filer with a part-year New York abode owes use tax on an item costing $1,000 or more, on business, rental or royalty purchases, or prefers the exact calculation, so must use Form ST-141 and truthfully answers yes, although no chart amount is prorated.
findings.source_text: ny_it201i p. 18, Line 59: "You must use Form ST-141 to calculate your sales and use tax liability ... if any of the following apply" and "multiply the tax amount from the chart by the number of months"
findings.why: Proration by months applies only to the chart amount. The gate is conditioned only on owing use tax and having a part-year abode, so a yes from an ST-141 filer triggers the chart-proration case when it does not apply.

findings.situation: A filer who lived outside New York City for all of 2025 (for example in Albany or Buffalo) truthfully answers no, and the gate treats them as a part-year New York City resident.
findings.source_text: ny_it201i p. 14, Line 50: "If you were a New York City resident for only part of 2025, complete Form IT-360.1"; ny_it201i p. 31: "You are a New York State nonresident if you were not a resident of New York State for any part of the year" (with New York City substituted)
findings.why: The gate sets part_year_city = (answer = false), and the question "Were you ... a New York City resident ... for all of 2025" gets the same no from full-year nonresidents of the City. Those filers owe no City resident tax and do not file Form IT-360.1, but the gate counts them as part-year City residents.

findings.situation: On a joint return where only one spouse was a full-year New York City resident, the filer cannot tell whether to answer yes or no to "you (and your spouse, on a joint return)".
findings.source_text: ny_it201i p. 14, Joint returns: "If you are married and filing a joint New York State return and only one of you was a resident of New York City for all of 2025, calculate on a separate sheet the New York City resident tax ... The spouse that was a part-year New York City resident in 2025 should: 1. Calculate their part-year New York City resident tax on Form IT-360.1"
findings.why: Some filers will read the parenthetical as asking about either spouse and others as asking about both, which gives different answers. The text also treats this mixed case on its own terms (a separate-sheet calculation, with Form IT-360.1 only when the other spouse was a part-year resident), and neither yes nor no matches that treatment.

findings.situation: A filer's estimated tax installment for one period was less than a quarter of the required annual payment, but enough tax was withheld from wages to cover that period, so nothing was underpaid for it.
findings.source_text: ny_it201i (2025) p. 23, Line 81: "You may owe an estimated tax penalty if you did not have enough tax withheld from your wages or did not make enough estimated tax payments ... We call these prepayments." and "if you underpaid your estimated tax liability for any payment period."
findings.why: The question asks only whether the installment itself was 'smaller than one quarter of the year's required payment.' The text measures underpayment for a period against all prepayments, including withholding, so this filer answers yes although no period was underpaid.

findings.situation: A filer with uneven income uses the annualized income installment method, so an early installment that is smaller than one quarter of the annual required payment is still the full amount required for that period.
findings.source_text: ny_it201i (2025) p. 23, Line 81: "if you underpaid your estimated tax liability for any payment period"; "For more information, see Form IT-2105.9"
findings.why: The question treats any installment below one quarter as short. Under the text, the test is whether the liability for that payment period was underpaid, so this filer truthfully answers yes although there was no underpayment.

findings.situation: A filer must decide what 'the year's required payment' means, for example the 2025 tax shown on the return, 90% of it, or 100% or 110% of the 2024 New York tax.
findings.source_text: ny_it201i (2025) p. 23, Line 81: "your 2025 prepayments must equal at least 110% of your 2024 New York income tax based on a 12-month return"; question: "smaller than one quarter of the year's required payment"
findings.why: The question and its help never define the required annual payment. Different reasonable readings give different quarter amounts, so the same installments can lead to a yes or a no.

findings.situation: A partner or S corporation shareholder whose only pass-through modifications are interest on non-New York state and local bonds (EA-113) or interest on U.S. government bonds (ES-125) would truthfully answer yes, although those amounts go on Form IT-201 lines 20 and 28 and not on Form IT-225.
findings.source_text: ny_it201i p. 7: "If you have either of the addition or subtraction modifications in the chart below, relating to your partnership or S corporation income, include the amount on the corresponding line of Form IT-201. ... EA-113 ... 20 ... ES-125 ... 28. For all other additions and subtractions relating to your partnership and S corporation income, complete Form IT-225."
findings.why: The question names "modifications passed through from a partnership, S corporation, estate or trust" without excluding EA-113 and ES-125. A filer with only those items opens the IT-225 gate even though no IT-225 entry is needed, and the amounts may also be counted on lines 20 and 28.

findings.situation: A filer with a valid extension who files by the extended due date but did not pay the full tax by April 15, 2026 owes interest, yet may answer no because they do not see themselves as filing or paying late.
findings.source_text: ny_it201i p. 24: "If you owe a late filing penalty, late payment penalty, or interest: ... Enter the penalty and interest amount on line 82."; "To avoid interest and penalty charges, you must file your return and pay the total amount you owe by April 15, 2026."
findings.why: The text needs a yes whenever any interest is owed, including interest on tax unpaid after April 15 during an extension. The question ties the answer to filing or paying 'late', so an extension filer who is on time for filing can truthfully answer no, and the gate is then wrongly left closed.

findings.situation: A filer who paid sales tax to one New York locality, then used the item in a New York locality with a higher rate where they lived at the time of purchase, owes additional local use tax but would answer no.

You owe use tax to the second locality if you were a resident of that locality at the time of the purchase, and its rate of tax is higher than the rate of tax originally paid."
findings.why: The question asks only about purchases made without paying New York tax, so a filer who paid some New York tax would truthfully answer no. Line 59 then gets 0 when a liability is owed.

findings.situation: A filer whose only unpaid use tax is on a motor vehicle, vessel, snowmobile or similar item, or on purchases of a business registered for sales tax, would answer yes, and line 59 would be filled from the chart.

findings.why: Neither the question nor its help excludes liabilities the text says must not be reported on line 59. A truthful yes on those purchases alone puts a chart amount on line 59 when the line should be 0.

findings.situation: A New York City part-year resident has income that was fixed in their 2025 City resident period but is reportable federally in their 2025 City nonresident period, so it is fixed and reported in the same tax year.
findings.source_text: ny_it201i p. 31: "income that was fixed and determinable in your 2025 New York City resident period, but that income is not reportable for federal income tax purposes in your 2025 New York City resident period; or • non-New York source income* that was fixed and determinable in your 2025 New York City nonresident period..."
findings.why: The question defines accrued income only as income 'fixed and determinable in one tax year but reported federally in another'. It misses accruals between the resident and nonresident periods within the same year.

findings.situation: A filer who lived in Buffalo all of 2024, 2025 and 2026 and has 2025 deferred compensation payable in 2026 would truthfully answer yes, because they were a New York City nonresident on December 31, 2024 and will be a City nonresident on January 1, 2026, but the rules do not apply to them.
findings.source_text: Question: "Were you a New York City nonresident on December 31, 2024, or will you be a New York State or City nonresident on January 1, 2026"; ny_it201i p. 31: "nonresident of New York City on December 31, 2024, but you were a full-year New York City resident for tax year 2025; or • full-year New York City resident for 2025 but you will be a New York City nonresident on January 1, 2026"; for State residents: "you were a nonresident of New York State on December 31, 2024; or • you will be a New York State nonresident on January 1, 2026."
findings.why: The City date tests apply only to someone who was a full-year or part-year New York City resident in 2025. As worded, the question is met by every upstate resident who never lived in the City.

findings.situation: A filer who moved into New York State from another state with New York-source income fixed in 2024 but reported federally in 2025 would answer yes, but only non-New York source income counts for that prior-year accrual.
findings.source_text: Question: "income fixed and determinable in one tax year but reported federally in another"; ny_it201i p. 31: "non-New York source income that was fixed and determinable in a tax year prior to 2025, but you are reporting that income for federal income tax purposes in tax year 2025"
findings.why: The question leaves out the non-New York source limit on income accrued in a prior year, so New York-source items that do not trigger the rules are brought in.

findings.situation: On a joint federal return, the spouse was a full-year New York State resident but lived outside New York City (or for only part of the year in it), so the filer truthfully answers no and the helper marks the spouse as not resident.
findings.source_text: ny_it201i p. 4, Item A: "One spouse is a New York State resident and the other is a nonresident or part-year resident."
findings.why: The cited exception depends only on New York State residency, but the question also requires New York City residency. A spouse who was a full-year State resident but not a City resident would be wrongly treated as falling under the separate-or-joint-as-residents exception.

findings.situation: A servicemember on active duty whose domicile is New York and who meets neither Group A nor Group B is a full-year resident, but the refusal list tells them to answer No.
findings.source_text: ny_it201i p. 30: "spend 184 days or more in New York State during the tax year*; whether or not you were domiciled in New York State (unless you were in active service in the military)" ... "Your domicile is New York State."
findings.why: The active-service exception applies only to the 184-day permanent-place-of-abode test, not to the domicile test. A New York-domiciled servicemember is still a resident who should file IT-201, yet the question's blanket instruction sends them to No and out through the part-year gate.

findings.situation: A full-time undergraduate whose domicile is New York and whose only New York residence is a dorm is a full-year resident, but the refusal list tells them to answer No.
findings.source_text: ny_it201i p. 30: "a residence maintained by a full-time student ... is not a permanent place of abode with respect to that student"; "Your domicile is New York State."
findings.why: The student-housing rule only stops the dorm from counting as a permanent place of abode. It does not undo residency by domicile, and a domiciled student who spends more than 30 days in New York cannot meet Group A, so they remain a resident.

findings.situation: On a joint return where one spouse was a full-year resident and the other was a nonresident or part-year resident, the couple may choose to file jointly on IT-201, but the wording requires both spouses to be residents, so they answer No.
findings.source_text: ny_it201i p. 3: "However, if you both choose to file a joint New York State return, use Form IT-201 and both spouses' income will be taxed as full-year residents of New York State."
findings.why: The text allows this mixed-residency couple to file IT-201 jointly. Because the question asks whether you and your spouse were both residents for all of 2025, these couples are gated out of a return the text allows.

findings.situation: A filer bought untaxed items for a business that is registered for sales tax, answers yes because the purchases were 'for a business', and the gate sends that tax to the Form ST-141 / line 59 path.
findings.source_text: ny_it201i p. 18: "You owe sales or use tax for purchases related to a business not registered for sales tax purposes, rental real estate, or royalty activities." and "You may not use this line to report: • any sales and use tax on business purchases if the business is registered for sales and use tax purposes. You must report this tax on the business's sales tax return."
findings.why: The question says 'purchases for a business' with no 'not registered for sales tax' qualifier. Use tax on a registered business's purchases must not go on line 59 at all, but a truthful yes brings it into the ST-141 gate.

findings.situation: A filer owes unpaid use tax on an out-of-state car, boat, trailer, ATV or snowmobile costing $1,000 or more, answers yes, and that tax is routed to Form ST-141 for line 59.
findings.source_text: ny_it201i p. 18: "You may not use this line to report: ... • any unpaid sales and use tax on motor vehicles, trailers, all-terrain vehicles, vessels, or snowmobiles. This tax is paid directly to the Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV)."
findings.why: The question ('an item or service costing $1,000 or more') and its help do not exclude these items. A truthful yes therefore brings in use tax the instructions bar from line 59.

findings.situation: A filer whose employer or a family member keeps a Yonkers apartment mainly for the filer's use, or who otherwise has use of Yonkers quarters someone else pays for, may truthfully answer no because they do not 'maintain' it themselves.
findings.source_text: ny_it201i p. 5, Item D2: "maintained or had use of an apartment or living quarters in Yonkers ... (whether or not you personally used those living quarters for any part of the year)"; "or that is maintained for your primary use by another person, family member, or employer."
findings.why: The question says only 'maintain living quarters'. It leaves out 'had use of' and quarters kept for the filer's primary use by an employer or family member. Those situations require a yes that a truthful filer may not give.

findings.situation: A married filer filing separately whose spouse kept Yonkers quarters, while the filer did not, would truthfully answer yes.
findings.source_text: Question: "Did you or your spouse maintain living quarters in Yonkers"; ny_it201i p. 5, Item D2: "If you or your spouse (if married filing jointly) maintained or had use of..."
findings.why: The text counts the spouse's quarters only on a joint return. The question counts the spouse under every filing status, so it brings in a yes the line must not have.

findings.situation: A filer with a $500 overpayment on line 77 who wants a larger amount, such as a full $2,000 quarterly installment, credited to 2026 estimated tax could enter $2,000, and the accepted answer would let it through.
findings.source_text: ny_it201i p. 23, Line 79: "Enter the amount of overpayment from line 77 that you want applied to ... estimated tax for 2026. The total of lines 78a through 79 should equal the amount on line 77."; Line 78: "Subtract the amount on line 79 (estimated tax) from line 77."
findings.why: Line 79 is a portion of line 77, so it cannot be more than line 77. The accepted answer has no upper limit, so line 78 (line 77 minus line 79) could go negative.
